questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: State what a member check can and cannot establish.
questions.stem: Ella Sanderson sent interview transcripts to the beekeepers who spoke to her and asks what their annotations establish.

options.text: That her coding is correct, since members approved the transcripts she sent them.
options.misconception: Treats participant sign-off as proof that the coding is right.

options.text: That members can recognise their own accounts and can point to where the reading misstates them.
That the accounts are representative of beekeepers across the whole region.
options.misconception: Believes a member check establishes representativeness.

options.text: That no further coding is needed, since the participants have signed off on the material.
options.misconception: Treats sign-off as an end to analysis.

questions.explanation: A member check gives participants the chance to contest how their words were read, which is evidence about the reading. It does not prove the coding correct, make the sample representative, or end the analysis.
questions.hint: A member check tests a reading, not the whole study.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a research journal entry as evidence about the researcher's practice.
questions.stem: Tomas Ruiz keeps a research journal alongside his field notes and reads back an entry that says he coded the third interview faster than the first.

options.text: The entry shows his coding sped up, which explains why later codes are thinner.
options.misconception: Reads a self-note as an excuse for weaker coding.

options.text: The entry shows his coding practice changed during the study, which belongs in the report.
The entry shows his journal is unreliable, so it should not be read at all.
options.misconception: Treats a candid note as a reason to discard it.

options.text: The entry shows the third interview contained less material than the first one did.
options.misconception: Reads a note about his own pace as a claim about the data.

questions.explanation: A journal entry that records his own change of pace is exactly the reflexive evidence the method exists to produce. It is not an excuse for weaker coding, a reason to discard the journal, or a statement about the interviews themselves.
questions.hint: A reflexive journal records the researcher, not the setting.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Justify a purposive sampling decision to a skeptical audience.
questions.stem: Grace Okonkwo must explain to her guild why she interviewed members of two clubs rather than every beekeeper nearby.

answer.exemplar: The justification should be that the two clubs were chosen because they differ in ways that matter to the question, for example colony size and the kind of forage nearby, so together they can show how the practice changes when the setting changes. A convenience sample of whoever was reachable would also be easy to defend operationally, but it would leave the reader unable to judge whether the account holds for other beekeepers, and the selection criteria have to be stated for that judgement to be possible.

questions.explanation: Purposive sampling earns its place by explaining why these cases were chosen, so a reader can judge scope. Convenience sampling is defensible operationally but leaves that judgement wide open.
questions.hint: Selection criteria have to be stated, not assumed.

questions.explanation: Three of the nine interviews added nothing new, so 9 minus 3, or 6, interviews shaped the codebook. The last three remain data; they simply did not change the scheme.
questions.hint: Subtract the interviews that changed nothing from the total.

options.text: He should plan the session so that less experienced voices get a route into the discussion.

options.text: Last, so the group has already built enough trust for the hard question.

options.misconception: Denies that order shapes what a group says.

options.text: Record his own reactions as they happen, then analyse how those reactions shaped his questions.

questions.learningObjective: Read a sampling decision recorded in a field log.

stimulus.body: From a guild study log: two colonies of about forty hives were chosen because one sits beside almond blossom and the other beside lime avenues, and members of both colonies were invited to two group discussions.

questions.stem: Imogen Croft reads the log and asks what the sampling decision does for her study.

options.text: It lets her compare how foraging conditions shape practice between the two groups.
It guarantees her findings describe beekeepers across the whole country.
options.misconception: Reads a two-case sample as national coverage.

options.text: It removes the need to report how participants were selected.
options.misconception: Believes purposeful choice excuses transparency.

options.text: It ensures the two groups will agree with each other in discussion.
options.misconception: Assumes matched groups will converge.

questions.explanation: Choosing two colonies that differ in their forage gives the study something to compare, so differences in practice can be traced to setting. That is not national coverage, a licence to skip reporting, or a guarantee of agreement.
questions.hint: Differences between cases are what make the sample useful.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a qualitative sample is not sized by a statistical calculation.
questions.stem: Daniel Osei must explain why a study of beekeepers was not sized by a statistical calculation.

answer.exemplar: The explanation should say that the sample is grown in the field until the analysis stops demanding new cases, not until a number computed in advance is reached. Saturation-based sizing therefore depends on the researcher's capacity to notice when a new interview would have added something, and it makes the stopping point a reportable decision rather than a hidden one. A fixed number borrowed from a formula would answer a different question, about estimating a quantity rather than about understanding a practice well enough to describe it.

questions.explanation: Saturation-based sizing grows the sample until new cases add nothing, so the stopping point is a judgment about sufficiency that has to be shown. A formula fixes a number but cannot say when understanding is enough.
questions.hint: The stopping rule is a reportable decision.

questions.stem: A focus group of 8 beekeepers ran for 90 minutes; 5 of them spoke during the first ten minutes. What percentage of the group had spoken by then?

questions.hint: Divide the speakers by the group size, then scale to a percent.

options.misconception: Abandons the check after one disagreement.

questions.explanation: A member contesting the record is a source of evidence about the reading, so it goes into the analysis rather than being deleted or argued away. Dropping the check because one member disagreed would make the method decorative.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret what a mixed sample of participants supports.

The mix proves his findings describe the national beekeeping population.
options.misconception: Reads a small mixed sample as population coverage.

options.text: The hobby beekeepers should be dropped, since they do not represent the trade.
options.misconception: Treats one group as the only legitimate case.

options.text: The counts should be equalised to 4 and 4 before any analysis starts.
options.misconception: Prescribes equal counts as the remedy for imbalance.

questions.explanation: Including both commercial and hobby beekeepers lets the study ask whether scale of operation changes how loss is described. It does not make the sample representative of the country, and the point of the mix is contrast rather than balance.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why recruitment continued past a fixed sample target.
questions.stem: Abel Tabor must explain why his study of beekeepers kept recruiting after a formal sample size target was reached.

answer.exemplar: The explanation should say that the target was a guide to effort, not a boundary on understanding, and that interviews continued because each new one still changed the account. A sample size fixed in advance answers a question about how precisely a quantity can be estimated; a qualitative study is trying to describe a practice and its variation well enough that the description does not fall apart on contact with a different colony. The point where nothing new appears is therefore part of the argument, and it has to be shown rather than asserted.

questions.explanation: Fixed targets estimate quantities; qualitative work asks whether the account still changes, so recruiting continues while cases still alter it. The stopping point belongs in the reasoning, not just the method section.
questions.hint: Say what the new cases were changing.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Group dynamics in a focus group
questions.learningObjective: Explain uneven talk and propose design changes.
questions.stem: Cleo Vance must explain to her guild why the talk in her group was uneven and what to do about it.

answer.exemplar: The explanation should link the imbalance to the shape of the group, since the two members with the most experience set the frame early and the others deferred to it, and to the size of the task, since a broad opening invited the confident to generalise. The remedies belong in the session design: a smaller or more homogeneous group, a written prompt that lets people think before speaking, a round in which everyone answers once, and a moderator who draws quieter members in by name rather than by open invitation.

questions.explanation: Uneven talk is produced by group composition and task shape, not by dull members, so remedies belong in the session design. Open invitations reward whoever spoke first, so turns must be made explicit.
questions.hint: Change the design that produces the imbalance.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Group dynamics in a focus group
questions.learningObjective: Explain persistent silence in a group session.
questions.stem: Nina Holm must explain why two beekeepers stayed silent in every one of her group sessions.

answer.exemplar: The explanation should treat silence as information about the setting rather than as a lack of interest, since the pair had spoken at length in the interviews and had taken the rear seats here, and had deferred to the loudest voice each time the topic came near their own operation. questions.explanation: Silence in a group can reflect who the room rewards rather than a lack of interest, especially when the same voices set the terms. Changing how turns and topics are framed addresses the cause.

options.misconception: Prescribes equal numbers as the goal of sampling.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a session note showing concentrated participation.

stimulus.body: From a session note: the moderator asked for the group's view, and the two most experienced members answered first every time, speaking for most of the ninety minutes while the remaining six members contributed a few short answers.

questions.stem: Carl Bengtsson reads the note and asks what the pattern indicates about the group.

options.text: That participation was concentrated and the session design needs to change.

options.misconception: Treats calm order as evidence of balanced participation.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Moderator and facilitator in a focus group
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the moderator and facilitator roles are kept apart.
questions.stem: Petra Vogel must explain to two new moderators why the roles of moderator and facilitator are kept apart.

answer.exemplar: The explanation should say that the moderator holds the analytic thread, asking the scheduled questions and pressing on the ones that carry the study, while the facilitator watches the group as a whole and acts on the room, drawing in a silent member, slowing a dominant one, or noting that time is running out. If one person holds both jobs, the questions get asked badly when the room needs managing, and the room gets mismanaged whenever a question needs following up. Keeping the roles apart protects the discussion from being run and observed at the same time by the same attention.

questions.explanation: Moderating holds the analytic thread while facilitating watches and acts on the room, and one person doing both drops whichever job is not in front of them. Separate roles protect both the discussion and the record.
questions.hint: Two jobs need two kinds of attention.

questions.learningObjective: Weigh the strength of member agreement according to the relationships involved.
questions.stem: Wim de Groot's member check produces agreement from members who were also in each other's groups.

options.text: Agreement from members who know each other is weaker evidence than agreement from strangers.

options.misconception: Treats any contact with participants as contamination.

options.text: He should ask members to check the work of each other instead of checking it himself.
options.misconception: Passes verification to participants rather than collecting it.

options.text: He should weight the agreeing members more heavily than the members who disagreed.
options.misconception: Invents a weighting that favours agreement.

questions.explanation: Agreement among people who already talk to each other is weaker evidence, since shared assumptions and mutual obligations can shape a response. Passing verification between members or weighting the agreeable responses adds nothing to what the check can show.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a journal entry that records a shift in coding.
questions.stem: Leila Mansour's journal shows she coded two interviews differently after hearing a member describe loss as a personal failure.

options.text: Her coding shifted after a member's framing, which belongs in the account of how the analysis was done.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Justify sampling participants whose practice has failed.
questions.stem: Arne Hjelm must justify interviewing beekeepers who have lost colonies rather than only successful ones.

options.text: That failure is where the practice is most visible and hardest to describe.
That failed colonies are plentiful, so they make an easy sample to recruit.
options.misconception: Justifies sampling by convenience of access.

options.text: That successful beekeepers have nothing worth saying about their losses.
options.misconception: Assumes success means silence on the topic.

options.text: That only failed colonies count as evidence of what causes colony loss.
options.misconception: Excludes the cases where the practice worked.

questions.explanation: Cases where a practice broke show the decisions and constraints in it most clearly, which is why they carry analytic weight. Ease of recruitment, dismissing the successful cases and treating only failures as evidence each miss that.

options.text: Because new interviews were still changing the account, which she can show.
Because saturation requires a fixed minimum number that she had not yet reached.

options.misconception: Explains the decision as an administrative convenience.

options.misconception: Treats a minority topic as noise to cut.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Moderator and facilitator in a focus group
questions.learningObjective: Write guidance that separates the two session roles.
questions.stem: Solveig Aas must write guidance for the moderators who will run her guild's sessions.

answer.exemplar: The guidance should say what each role does and what each must refuse to do. The moderator keeps the analytic thread: the scheduled questions, the follow-ups that press on a point, and the summary at the end that the group can correct. The facilitator keeps the room in view: noticing that one member has not spoken, that another has taken over, that the energy has dropped, and acting on it by name rather than by general appeal. Writing also what each should not do prevents the two jobs from sliding into one another, which is where sessions usually go wrong.

questions.explanation: Guidance should define both roles and set boundaries, since sessions fail when the jobs merge. Naming members directly, not appealing generally, is what balances participation.
questions.hint: Define the roles and what each must refuse to do.

questions.topic: Question order in a focus group
questions.learningObjective: Explain why question order in a group session is a method decision.
questions.stem: Chidi Eze must explain to his guild why the order of questions in a group session is not arbitrary.

answer.exemplar: The explanation should say that questions in a group are answered in relation to what has just been said, so the broad opener sets the frame and gives less confident members something to react to, the follow-ups then probe the accounts that the group itself raised, and the sharper questions on disagreement come last, once members have invested in the conversation and have heard their own words quoted back. Put the hard question first and the group answers it in generalities, or argues about what it means, and the rest of the session never gets to the specific detail the researcher needed.

questions.explanation: Questions in a group are answered in relation to what came before, so broad material first gives later hard questions something to bite on. Sequence is a method decision, not a convenience.

options.text: She should share only the parts about the beekeepers, protecting herself from scrutiny.
options.misconception: Assumes reflexivity requires self-exposure to the participants.

questions.explanation: A journal written as the work proceeds records thinking while it is still forming, which is what later readers need to see. Reconstructing it from memory, keeping it thin or editing the self out of it each remove the thing the method is for.
questions.hint: The value is in the process, not the reconstruction.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Interpret what a purposive sample of differing cases supports.
questions.stem: Ida Fenwick's purposive sample includes 2 large honey producers, 5 small orchard beekeepers and 3 hobbyists.

options.text: The three kinds of case were chosen for the differences that bear on her question.
The sample is too small, because no qualitative study can use fewer than ten cases.
options.misconception: Invents a minimum sample size for qualitative work.

options.text: The hobbyists should be replaced with more orchard beekeepers to balance the groups.
options.misconception: Prescribes equal numbers instead of relevant differences.

options.text: The sample should have been drawn at random, because purposive choice always favours the argument.
options.misconception: Treats any selection as advocacy.

questions.explanation: The kinds of case were picked because they differ in ways that bear on the question, and that is what makes the sample worth the effort of analysing. A minimum count, equal numbers and a preference for random selection each miss what purposive choice is doing.
questions.hint: Ask what each kind of case is there to do.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Defend the sizing decision in a qualitative study.
questions.stem: Amara Sissoko must defend her decision about how many beekeepers to interview.

options.text: She should show that new cases stopped changing the account and that she kept adding while they did.
She should show that the number matched a standard set for studies of this kind.
options.misconception: Defends sizing by appeal to a rule rather than evidence.

options.text: She should show that the number was large enough for the comparisons she wants to make.
options.misconception: Justifies qualitative sizing with statistical logic.

options.text: She should show that the participants were available and willing, since that is what limits a field study.
options.misconception: Offers convenience as the justification.

questions.explanation: Sizing is defended by the rule she followed and the evidence that it was reached, namely cases that stopped changing the account while she kept adding until then. A standard, a statistical comparison and availability describe constraints or conventions instead.
questions.hint: Show the rule and the evidence for it.
